cards.definition: Know your audience and what they value, and deliver on what you promise.
Opt-in requires the customer to choose to receive something. Opt-out requires the customer to choose to stop receiving it.

A second item can seem more different from the first than it really is. Comparing two things can make one seem better or less bad; for example, mentioning much larger awards first can make $10,000 seem small.
Repay in kind what others give us. Because societies teach this rule, giving something first can create a strong obligation to give back.
Help customers without expecting an immediate return and trust that the goodwill will eventually come back to you.

cards.term: Utilitarian maximization of good in sales
cards.definition: Choose the sales tactic that creates the greatest total benefit for everyone involved.

Automaticity is a click-whirr response triggered by a single feature. Animals have instinctive fixed-action patterns; humans also have automatic tapes, but theirs come from learned principles rather than instinct.
The tendency to rely on an authority figure.

cards.term: Automatic responding: benefit, risk, and safeguard
cards.definition: Automatic responding is efficient, but it can be triggered at the wrong time. Rushing, stress, and distraction strengthen shortcuts, so slowing the environment gives people time to think.
Mechanical activation, exploitability, and the ability to manipulate people without appearing to do so.

Make a larger request first, then retreat to the smaller request you actually want. The first request should not be so extreme that it seems illegitimate. The retreat looks like a concession, creating pressure to reciprocate, while contrast makes the second request seem smaller.
The rule can overpower other factors, create debts from uninvited favors, and produce unfair exchanges.
The study showed reciprocity's exploitable features: liking did not matter, participants did not ask for the Coke, and a 10-cent Coke produced about 50 cents in ticket purchases.

People want to be and appear consistent with prior actions. Consistency is associated with logic, stability, and honesty, and it acts as a shortcut because a decision reduces the need to keep thinking about it.
A commitment is strongest when it is active, public, effortful, and freely chosen.

cards.term: Commitment and consistency tactics in sales
cards.definition: Foot-in-the-door, written commitments, and lowballing.
They provide physical proof, can be made public, and require more effort.

cards.term: Lowballing and growing its own leg
cards.definition: A commitment creates new justifications for the decision, so the original lowball incentive can be removed and the decision may still stand.
People decide what is correct by observing what others do. Canned laughter illustrates this principle because laugh tracks can make audiences laugh more and rate material as funnier.
Social proof has the greatest influence under uncertainty and when the other people are similar to the observer.
People look to others for clues during an emergency; when no one reacts, everyone may assume that the situation is not an emergency.

cards.term: City conditions that reduce bystander intervention
cards.definition: Confusing environments, having more people present, and being surrounded mostly by strangers.
Listen to the objection, acknowledge it, explore it with questions to identify the real concern, and then respond.
